claims.text: The initial material is a solid refractory material at room temperature.
A computational method based on machine-learning potentials can accurately predict refractory-material melting properties.
The method can predict melting temperature, entropy of fusion, enthalpy of fusion, and volume change at the melting point.
The MLP method has lower computational cost than the DFT-based ab initio free-energy approach.
The proposed application concerns refractory materials with melting temperatures above 2000 K.
The method is suitable for high-throughput calculations.
MLPs learn the material's potential-energy surface from atomic configurations.
MLP training minimizes differences between predicted and reference energies for atomic configurations.
Predicted melting temperatures will be within 10 K of experimental values.
Predicted entropies of fusion will be within 0.05 J mol^-1 K^-1 of experimental values.
Predicted enthalpies of fusion will be within 0.05 kJ mol^-1 of experimental values.
Predicted volume changes at melting will be within 0.02 cm^3 mol^-1 of experimental values.
The MLPs are trained using a dataset containing at least 100 refractory materials with experimentally determined melting properties.
The training dataset covers a range of chemical compositions and crystal structures.
Prediction accuracy depends on the quality and diversity of the training dataset.
Prediction accuracy may depend on the complexity of the refractory material's atomic structure.
The hypothesis is falsified if melting-temperature MAE exceeds 10%.
The hypothesis is falsified if entropy-of-fusion or enthalpy-of-fusion MAE exceeds 5%.
The hypothesis is falsified if volume-change MAE exceeds 2%.

contradictions.description: The outcome claims use stringent absolute-error limits, whereas falsification uses percentage MAE limits. These criteria are not equivalent and can permit acceptance even when the stated absolute-error predictions fail; for example, a melting-temperature MAE below 10% can still greatly exceed 10 K above 2000 K.

The mechanism describes a potential-energy model trained against configuration-level reference energies, while the boundary describes training on experimentally determined melting properties across materials. The relationship between these different training targets and datasets is not explained.
